description:
Is That Seriously Smoke? 

We're a small team interested in Earth science and software development, working on a project that uses NASA satellite data to help detect and track wildfire activity. We're excited to apply our combined interest in data, coding, and environmental problems to build something useful during this challenge.
summary:
We developed an interactive web map of wildfire activity in Quebec from 2000 to today, built on NASA FIRMS data.

Fires have been recorded from orbit by MODIS since 2000 and by the sharper VIIRS sensor since 2012. VIIRS reports several times more detections for the same fire, so raw counts  from 2005 and 2024 measure different things. We convert detections into fire activity (10 km squares burning per day), fit a correction curve on the years both sensors were flying, and apply it to the earlier record. Pre-2012 values are shown as estimates with a likely range, and we validate the method by hiding each year in turn and checking the estimate against what VIIRS actually recorded.

Users can play back 25 years of fire activity, search any place, view statistics and the hardest-hit areas, see a risk outlook based on past seasons and recent weather, download the data, and share any view.

  This matters because understanding whether fire activity is really changing requires a consistent long-term record. Our tool makes that record accessible to communities,
  journalists, students and decision makers, not only scientists.
details:
Our project is an interactive map of every satellite fire detection in Quebec from November 2000 to today, 723,108 points in all. It's built for emergency responders and planners who need to know how fire activity at a place compares with the past. You can play the record month by month, pick any period, and search for a town or type in coordinates. A side panel then tells you how much fire there has been within 50, 100 or 200 km, how that compares with other years, and which areas were hit hardest.

The hard part is that the 26-year record comes from two different satellite cameras. MODIS has been flying since 2000. VIIRS was added in 2012, and it's sharper, so it reports about 5.6 times as many hotspots for the same fires. If you put raw counts from 2005 and 2024 on the same chart, the chart shows a camera upgrade, not a change in fire. Most fire maps never deal with this. We did:

1. A common format. We merged six NASA FIRMS datasets (MODIS, VIIRS Suomi NPP and VIIRS NOAA-20, both archive and recent files) into one table. Where a dataset has no value for a field, we flag the gap instead of hiding it. We also removed fixed industrial heat sources such as smelters and mills, which turned out to be about half of the recent unlabelled detections.

2. A better unit. We count "fire activity": the number of ~10 km map squares that burned, counted once for each day they burned. On this measure the gap between the cameras shrinks from 5.6× to about 1.6×.

3. A correction. For the years when both cameras were flying, we fitted a curve that converts older-camera activity to the newer camera's level. All months before 2012 are shown as estimates with a likely range. Measured months are never changed.

4. A test. We hid each year from 2012 to 2025 in turn, fitted the curve on the other years, and predicted the hidden year. The median error was 15% with our curve, 30% with a single fixed multiplier, and 57% with no correction. The page shows these results, including the years where the method did poorly, so users can judge how far to trust it.

On top of the record, the map gives a risk outlook for the next two weeks at any place: low, usual or high. It starts from how fire-prone those two weeks have been in past seasons. Recent fire activity and recent weather from NASA POWER (rainfall and temperature compared with normal) can move it up or down by one level. Every level comes with a plain-language reason. We deliberately didn't call it a prediction or draw fire spread, because a wrong forecast shown to responders is worse than none.


Benefits and intended impact

- Quebec's fire history becomes one consistent record, so you can actually compare 2023 with 2005.

- Uncertainty stays visible. Estimates look different from measurements and always come with a range.

- Anyone can use it. It runs in a browser with no login or key, every view is a shareable link, the data downloads as CSV, and the animation can be saved as a video for briefings.

- Places outside Quebec are fetched from NASA on demand, so the same tool works elsewhere in Canada.

Tools and technologies

- Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20), NASA POWER daily weather

- Backend: Python with pandas, NumPy, Shapely, PyArrow/Parquet, FastAPI, httpx and pytest

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, deck.gl (all 723k points are filtered on the graphics card, so playback stays smooth), Vitest

- Base map and search: CARTO base map and OpenStreetMap Nominatim, neither of which needs a key

- Deployment: Docker on Google Cloud Run, with the NASA key kept on the server in Secret Manager

How is our project creative?

We treated the satellite record as a problem to solve, not just data to plot. NASA has watched Quebec burn for 26 years, but through two cameras that see differently. The newer one reports more than five times as many hotspots for the same fire. Every map that puts both on one timeline quietly overstates how much worse fires have become since 2012. Our creative step was to stitch the two into one continuous record, the way climate scientists join temperature readings from old and new thermometers.

To do that, we stopped counting dots. A sharper camera sees more dots, but it doesn't see more burning land. So we measure fire as "how many 10 km squares burned, and for how many days". That one change of unit cut the gap between the cameras from 5.6× to 1.6×. A fitted curve closes the rest.

Then we tried to prove ourselves wrong. We hid each year from the model, had it predict that year blind, and published the results, including the year it missed by 65%. Every number from before 2012 carries a range rather than a single value. It's a fire map that tells you how far to trust it.

We were just as careful with prediction. The team wanted to forecast fires. In a weekend, an honest fire-spread forecast wasn't possible, and a confident wrong one could sendresponders the wrong way. So we built an outlook that answers a question we can answer: are the next two weeks usually dangerous here, and is this year drier or more active than usual? It combines two NASA datasets, FIRMS for fire and POWER for weather, and gives a reason in plain words for every level it reports.

Factors we considered

- Honesty over impressiveness. Every estimate has an error range, and the outlook explains each step of its reasoning.

- Fit for responders. Plain language, fast loading, a link that keeps showing the latest data, and nothing that looks like live information when it isn't.

- Scope. The correction is only valid for an area over a month or more, not for a single square on a single day, and the app says so.

- Cost and security. No API keys in the browser, a single small server, and free map and search services.
